nodeData.topic: 🧬 Year 2 · Body in health and disease

children.note: Advanced systems physiology — kidney, acid–base, gut, endocrine, reproduction, neurophysiology and special senses — underpinning care of diabetes, dehydration, pregnancy and neurological illness in Kenya.

Advanced lipid, amino acid, haem and nucleotide metabolism, molecular biology, hormone signalling and nutrition — linking biochemistry to jaundice, malnutrition, drug action and molecular diagnostics.
Principles of laboratory testing and interpretation of electrolytes, acid–base, renal, liver, glucose, bone and protein tests — the everyday results a doctor in Kenya must read correctly.
Foundations of bacteriology, virology and mycology: microbial structure, growth, genetics, sterilisation, antibiotics and resistance, and key bacterial pathogens seen in Kenyan practice.

Basic immunology: cells and organs of immunity, innate defences, complement, antibodies, antigen presentation, T and B cells, cytokines and tolerance – the basis for understanding infection and vaccines.
Principles of pharmacology — pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, adverse reactions, interactions and autonomic drugs — the basis for safe prescribing by every doctor in Kenya.

The general mechanisms of disease: cell injury, inflammation, repair, circulatory disorders, immune injury and neoplasia. The language every Kenyan clinician needs to reason about TB, malaria, cancer and more.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to long-chain acyl-CoA, so the acyl group is passed to carnitine.

manas.q: Why do long-chain fatty acids need carnitine?

children.note: CPT-I makes acylcarnitine; a translocase swaps it in for free carnitine; CPT-II on the inner membrane remakes acyl-CoA.

manas.q: What are the three steps of the carnitine shuttle?

children.note: Short and medium-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria without carnitine.

manas.q: Which fatty acids enter mitochondria without carnitine?

children.note: From the diet, especially meat, and made in the body from lysine and methionine.

manas.q: From which amino acids is carnitine made?

children.note: Four reactions repeat each cycle.
Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase forms a trans double bond between C2 and C3, reducing FAD to FADH2.

manas.q: Which coenzyme is reduced in the first step of β-oxidation?

children.note: Enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water across the double bond to give L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA.

manas.q: What does enoyl-CoA hydratase produce?

children.note: 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidises the hydroxyl group to a ketone, reducing NAD+ to NADH.

manas.q: Which step of β-oxidation produces NADH?

children.note: Thiolase uses CoA to cut off acetyl-CoA, leaving an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter for the next cycle.

manas.q: What does thiolase release in each cycle?

children.note: Separate acyl-CoA dehydrogenases act on very long, long, medium and short chains (VLCAD, LCAD, MCAD, SCAD).

manas.q: Why are there several acyl-CoA dehydrogenases?

children.note: For long chains, one inner-membrane complex carries out steps 2–4, including long-chain hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD).

manas.q: Which enzyme activity of the trifunctional protein is LCHAD?

children.note: C16 palmitate needs 7 cycles, giving 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH2 and 7 NADH.

manas.q: How many cycles of β-oxidation does palmitate need?

children.note: Need extra enzymes: an enoyl-CoA isomerase and, for many polyunsaturated ones, 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase using NADPH.

manas.q: Which extra enzymes oxidise unsaturated fatty acids?

children.note: Burn fat or make fat, not both.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA in the fed state; malonyl-CoA blocks CPT-I, so new fat is not burned at once.

manas.q: How does malonyl-CoA prevent a futile cycle?

children.note: Insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase (more malonyl-CoA, less oxidation); glucagon inhibits it (more oxidation).

manas.q: How does glucagon increase fatty acid oxidation?

children.note: When energy is low, AMP-activated kinase phosphorylates and inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, lowering malonyl-CoA.

manas.q: How does AMPK increase fatty acid oxidation?

children.note: A nuclear receptor that switches on genes for fatty acid oxidation in fasting; fibrates act through it.

manas.q: Which nuclear receptor do fibrates activate?

children.note: Liver turns excess acetyl-CoA into fuel.
In fasting or uncontrolled diabetes, hepatic oxaloacetate goes to gluconeogenesis, so acetyl-CoA builds up and forms ketones.

manas.q: Why does acetyl-CoA form ketones in fasting?

children.note: Acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase, rate-limiting) → acetoacetate.

manas.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis?

children.note: Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate (made from it using NADH) and acetone (formed spontaneously, breathed out).

manas.q: Name the three ketone bodies.

children.note: The liver lacks succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase (thiophorase), so it exports ketones to other tissues.

manas.q: Why can the liver not use ketone bodies?

children.note: Urine nitroprusside strips detect acetoacetate (and acetone) but not β-hydroxybutyrate, the main ketone in DKA.

manas.q: Which ketone body is not detected by nitroprusside strips?

children.note: Peroxisomes, ER and odd chains.
Peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase passes electrons straight to oxygen, making H2O2 instead of FADH2; shortened chains go to mitochondria.

manas.q: How does the first step of peroxisomal β-oxidation differ?

children.note: Branched phytanic acid is shortened by one carbon in peroxisomes; its failure causes Refsum disease.

manas.q: Which disease results from defective α-oxidation of phytanic acid?

children.note: In the endoplasmic reticulum, cytochrome P450 oxidises the far end, making dicarboxylic acids; it rises when β-oxidation fails.

manas.q: Where does ω-oxidation occur and what does it produce?

children.note: Lack of B12 blocks methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so methylmalonic acid rises: a useful test of B12 deficiency.

manas.q: Why does methylmalonic acid rise in B12 deficiency?

children.note: Beyond MCAD basics.
Illness or fasting brings hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, lethargy, liver enlargement and sometimes high ammonia.

manas.q: What is the typical metabolic picture of a fatty acid oxidation defect?

children.note: VLCAD, LCHAD and trifunctional protein defects can also cause cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

manas.q: Which extra features do long-chain oxidation defects cause?

children.note: A mother carrying an LCHAD-deficient fetus is at risk of acute fatty liver of pregnancy and HELLP syndrome.

manas.q: Which pregnancy complications are linked to fetal LCHAD deficiency?

children.note: The adult muscle form causes attacks of muscle pain and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria after exercise or fasting.

manas.q: How does the adult form of CPT-II deficiency present?

children.note: Liver form: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in infancy, with normal or high free carnitine.

manas.q: What happens to free carnitine in CPT-I deficiency?

children.note: Faulty OCTN2 carnitine transporter (SLC22A5) causes very low carnitine and cardiomyopathy; carnitine supplements treat it.

manas.q: Which transporter is defective in primary carnitine deficiency?

children.note: Low carnitine from other causes, e.g. valproate, dialysis or organic acidaemias.

manas.q: Name causes of secondary carnitine deficiency.

children.note: Hypoglycin A in unripe ackee fruit inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, causing severe hypoglycaemia.

manas.q: What causes Jamaican vomiting sickness?

children.note: Catch the sample during the attack.
Tandem mass spectrometry of blood shows which acylcarnitine builds up, e.g. octanoylcarnitine (C8) in MCAD deficiency.

manas.q: Which acylcarnitine is raised in MCAD deficiency?

children.note: Dicarboxylic aciduria with little ketone suggests a β-oxidation defect.

manas.q: What urine organic acid pattern suggests a β-oxidation defect?

children.note: During hypoglycaemia, before treatment if possible: glucose, ketones, free fatty acids, insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, lactate, ammonia and acylcarnitines (plus urine organic acids).

manas.q: Which tests make up the critical sample in hypoglycaemia?

children.note: Enzyme or gene testing confirms the defect; carnitine levels help separate primary from secondary deficiency.

manas.q: How is a fatty acid oxidation defect confirmed?

children.note: Prevent fasting, treat early.
Frequent feeds and a written emergency plan with glucose drinks or IV dextrose during illness.

manas.q: What is the key preventive measure in fatty acid oxidation defects?

children.note: In long-chain defects, a low long-chain fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides bypasses the block; avoid MCT in MCAD.

manas.q: Why are medium-chain triglycerides avoided in MCAD deficiency?

children.note: Carnitine supplements are the main treatment for primary carnitine deficiency.

manas.q: What treats primary carnitine deficiency?

children.note: Quick points examiners like.
Low glucose with low ketones means fat cannot be burned or ketones made: think fatty acid oxidation defect or hyperinsulinism.

manas.q: What two causes should hypoketotic hypoglycaemia suggest?

children.note: Even-chain fatty acids give acetyl-CoA, and pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so no net glucose forms.

manas.q: Why can even-chain fatty acids not make net glucose?

children.note: 8 acetyl-CoA × 10 + 7 NADH × 2.5 + 7 FADH2 × 1.5 = 108; minus 2 for activation = 106.

manas.q: How is the 106 ATP from palmitate calculated?

children.note: Acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation activates pyruvate carboxylase, supporting gluconeogenesis in fasting.

manas.q: Which enzyme does acetyl-CoA activate to support gluconeogenesis?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-09.
A review describes fasting liver fat oxidation and ketogenesis driven by hormones and rising fatty acids, acting through PPAR-α; women tend to have higher ketones.

manas.q: Which transcription factor mediates fasting hepatic fatty acid oxidation, per a 2024 review?

children.note: In 757 reported patients, cardiac problems (mainly cardiomyopathy, 23.8%) were the commonest feature; most screen-detected people stayed well, but rare sudden severe events occurred.

manas.q: What was the most common feature of primary carnitine deficiency in a 2022 review?

nodeData.topic: Drug development and nomenclature in depth
nodeData.note: From a new molecule to a licensed, named medicine: discovery, trials, regulation and how drugs get their names. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The big picture of how a medicine reaches patients.
Drug development is the staged process of discovering a compound, testing it in the lab and in people, licensing it and monitoring it after launch.

manas.q: What are the main stages of drug development?

children.note: Discovery → preclinical testing → clinical trial phases I–III → regulatory approval → phase IV post-marketing surveillance.

manas.q: Put the stages of drug development in order.

children.note: Most candidate compounds fail during development, mainly because of poor efficacy or unacceptable toxicity; the process is long and costly.

manas.q: Why do most candidate drugs never reach the market?

children.note: Where new drugs come from.
A molecular target linked to disease (receptor, enzyme, ion channel, transporter) is chosen, and compounds are screened against it.

manas.q: What is the first step in rational drug discovery?

children.note: A promising 'lead' compound is chemically modified to improve potency, selectivity and drug-like properties before testing.

manas.q: What is a lead compound?

children.note: Many drugs began as plant products, e.g. morphine from the opium poppy, digoxin from foxglove, quinine from cinchona bark.

manas.q: Name a drug derived from a plant and its source.

children.note: Most modern drugs are synthetic; biologics such as recombinant human insulin and monoclonal antibodies are made by biotechnology.

manas.q: How is modern human insulin produced?

children.note: Lab and animal work before any human dose.
Tests pharmacology, pharmacokinetics and toxicity in cells, tissues and animals to judge whether human testing is reasonably safe.

manas.q: What does preclinical testing assess?

children.note: Include acute and repeat-dose toxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity and reproductive toxicity testing.

manas.q: Name types of preclinical toxicology study.

children.note: Animal results do not always predict human responses, so the first human doses are small and closely watched.

manas.q: Why are first human doses kept small?

children.note: Testing in people, step by step.
Optional, very small sub-therapeutic doses in a few people to study pharmacokinetics early; no therapeutic aim.

manas.q: What is a phase 0 study?

children.note: Usually healthy volunteers; finds a safe dose range. Exception: toxic drugs such as anticancer agents are first given to patients.

manas.q: When is phase I done in patients instead of healthy volunteers?

children.note: Small groups of patients with the target disease; first evidence of efficacy and the dose to take forward.

manas.q: What is the purpose of phase II trials?

children.note: Large, often multicentre randomised trials in patients; confirm efficacy and safety against placebo or standard care.

manas.q: What is the typical design of a phase III trial?

children.note: After licensing; spontaneous reporting systems and observational studies pick up rare, delayed and interaction effects.

manas.q: Why are rare adverse effects often found only in phase IV?

children.note: How trials are made fair and safe.
Random allocation to groups balances known and unknown confounders and reduces selection bias.

manas.q: What bias does randomisation reduce?

children.note: In double-blind trials neither participants nor investigators know the allocation, reducing performance and assessment bias.

manas.q: What does double-blind mean?

children.note: Placebo controls show true drug effect; when good treatment exists, comparing with standard therapy is more ethical.

manas.q: When is an active comparator preferred to placebo?

children.note: Participants are analysed in the group they were randomised to, whatever happened later, preserving randomisation.

manas.q: What is intention-to-treat analysis?

children.note: Participants must freely agree after understanding risks, benefits and their right to withdraw at any time.

manas.q: What must participants understand before giving informed consent?

children.note: An independent research ethics committee must approve a trial before it starts and oversee it.

manas.q: Who must approve a clinical trial before it begins?

children.note: World Medical Association statement of ethical principles for medical research involving humans.

manas.q: Which document sets ethical principles for human research?

children.note: International standard (ICH-GCP) for designing, running, recording and reporting trials ethically and reliably.

manas.q: What is Good Clinical Practice?

children.note: Licensing and watching medicines.
A regulator licenses a medicine after reviewing evidence of quality, safety and efficacy and judging benefit outweighs risk.

manas.q: What three things must a regulator be satisfied about?

children.note: Detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse effects of medicines after they are in use.

manas.q: Define pharmacovigilance.

children.note: Health workers report suspected adverse drug reactions and poor-quality medicines to the Pharmacy and Poisons Board.

manas.q: To whom are suspected adverse drug reactions reported in Kenya?

children.note: After the patent expires, other makers can sell generics, usually much cheaper, which widens access.

manas.q: When can generic versions of a drug be marketed?

children.note: A generic must show bioequivalence: similar rate and extent of absorption to the original product.

manas.q: What must a generic drug show to be approved?

children.note: Regulators classify medicines as prescription-only or available over the counter according to their risk.

manas.q: On what basis are medicines classed as prescription-only?

children.note: One drug, several names.
Describes the exact chemical structure; long and rarely used clinically.

manas.q: What does a drug's chemical name describe?

children.note: A letters-and-numbers label a company gives a compound during development.

manas.q: What is a drug's code name?

children.note: Non-proprietary name chosen by the WHO INN Programme; unique and recognised worldwide.

manas.q: Who assigns International Nonproprietary Names?

children.note: Trademark name chosen by a manufacturer, written with a capital letter; one drug can have many brands.

manas.q: How is a brand name written and who chooses it?

children.note: INN paracetamol is called acetaminophen in the USA; it is sold under many brand names.

manas.q: What is the US name for paracetamol?

children.note: Clearer communication, less confusion between brands, and usually cheaper medicines.

manas.q: Give two reasons to prescribe by generic name.

children.note: Drug names that look or sound similar are a known cause of medication errors; write clearly and check.

manas.q: Why are look-alike, sound-alike drug names dangerous?

children.note: Common endings that reveal the drug class.
Beta-adrenoceptor blockers, e.g. propranolol, atenolol.

manas.q: Which drug class ends in -olol?

children.note: ACE inhibitors, e.g. enalapril, captopril.

manas.q: Which drug class ends in -pril?

children.note: Angiotensin II receptor blockers, e.g. losartan.

manas.q: Which drug class ends in -sartan?

children.note: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors that lower cholesterol, e.g. atorvastatin.

manas.q: What do drugs ending in -statin inhibit?

children.note: Proton pump inhibitors, e.g. omeprazole.

manas.q: Which drug class ends in -prazole?

children.note: Penicillin antibiotics, e.g. amoxicillin.

manas.q: Which antibiotic group ends in -cillin?

children.note: Local anaesthetics, e.g. lidocaine.

manas.q: Which drug class ends in -caine?

children.note: Antiviral drugs, e.g. aciclovir, tenofovir.

manas.q: What kind of drug ends in -vir?

children.note: Grouping drugs and drugs that need activating.
By therapeutic use, by mechanism or pharmacological action, or by chemical structure.

manas.q: Name three ways drugs are classified.

children.note: The well-known representative of a class, used to learn the class's actions and adverse effects.

manas.q: What is a prototype drug?

children.note: Prodrug that crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain.

manas.q: Why is levodopa given instead of dopamine?

children.note: Prodrug activated in the liver, mainly by CYP2C19; poor metabolisers get less antiplatelet effect.

manas.q: Which enzyme activates clopidogrel?

children.note: When development fails patients.
Used in pregnancy in the late 1950s–early 1960s, it caused limb defects (phocomelia) and led to much stricter drug regulation.

manas.q: What birth defect did thalidomide cause?

children.note: Pre-licensing trials cannot detect very rare adverse reactions, so post-marketing surveillance is essential.

manas.q: Why can't phase III trials detect very rare adverse effects?

children.note: Children, pregnant women and older people are often excluded from trials, so evidence for them is limited.

manas.q: Which groups are often under-represented in drug trials?

children.note: Medicines that fail quality standards or deliberately misrepresent identity or source harm patients and drive resistance.

manas.q: What are falsified medicines?

children.note: Bodies a student should recognise.
The Pharmacy and Poisons Board registers medicines, licenses premises and runs pharmacovigilance.

manas.q: What does Kenya's Pharmacy and Poisons Board do?

children.note: WHO assesses medicines' quality, safety and efficacy so UN agencies and countries can buy them with confidence.

manas.q: What is WHO prequalification for?

children.note: The Food and Drug Administration licenses medicines in the United States.

manas.q: Which body licenses medicines in the USA?

children.note: The European Medicines Agency evaluates medicines for authorisation across the European Union.

manas.q: Which agency evaluates medicines for the EU?

children.note: The International Council for Harmonisation aligns technical requirements, e.g. GCP, across regulators.

manas.q: What does the ICH harmonise?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-18.
A review notes the AU's African Medicines Agency has a treaty signed by 37 states and a chosen headquarters, but weak financing and laws in some states slow it.

manas.q: What slows the African Medicines Agency, per a 2024 review?

children.note: WHO stopped using -mab for new antibody INNs in 2021, replacing it with four stems: -tug, -bart, -mig and -ment.

manas.q: Which four stems replaced -mab for new antibody names?

children.note: A 2023 review found expedited development and approval pathways for drugs of high unmet need are increasingly available across ICH countries, so sponsors must rethink submission strategy.

manas.q: What trend in approval pathways did a 2023 review describe?

children.note: Quick wins.
I = safety and PK; II = efficacy and dose; III = confirm against comparator; IV = post-marketing safety.

manas.q: State the main purpose of each trial phase.

children.note: Phase I usually; phases II–III always use patients.

manas.q: Which trial phase usually uses healthy volunteers?

children.note: Generic (INN) name is lower case and global; brand name is capitalised and company-owned.

manas.q: How do you tell a generic name from a brand name?

children.note: Learn -olol, -pril, -sartan, -statin, -prazole; they reveal the class from the name.

manas.q: What does the stem of a drug name tell you?

nodeData.note: How cells change size, number or type under stress, why it happens, and when adaptation turns pre-malignant. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Where adaptation sits in the response to stress.
Reversible changes in cell size, number, type or function that let cells survive altered demands or harmful stimuli.

manas.q: What is a cellular adaptation?

children.note: Normal cell → adaptation → reversible injury → irreversible injury and cell death, as stress rises or persists.

manas.q: Describe the spectrum of cell responses to increasing stress.

children.note: Physiological adaptations answer normal demands (hormones, exercise); pathological ones answer disease or injury.

manas.q: What separates physiological from pathological adaptation?

children.note: Hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy and metaplasia; dysplasia is disordered growth, not a true adaptation.

manas.q: Name the four main cellular adaptations.

children.note: Bigger cells, bigger organ.
Increase in cell size from more structural proteins and organelles, enlarging the organ without new cells.

manas.q: What causes organ enlargement in hypertrophy?

children.note: Cardiac and skeletal muscle cells divide little, so they adapt to load mainly by hypertrophy.

manas.q: Why do cardiac myocytes adapt by hypertrophy rather than hyperplasia?

children.note: Mechanical stretch sensors, growth factors and vasoactive agents switch on signalling that boosts muscle protein synthesis.

manas.q: What triggers hypertrophy signalling in muscle?

children.note: Hypertrophied heart muscle re-expresses fetal genes, e.g. atrial natriuretic peptide and β-myosin heavy chain.

manas.q: Which fetal genes are re-expressed in cardiac hypertrophy?

children.note: Skeletal muscle in weight training; uterine smooth muscle in pregnancy (with hyperplasia).

manas.q: Give a physiological example of hypertrophy.

children.note: Left ventricular hypertrophy from pressure overload, e.g. systemic hypertension or aortic stenosis.

manas.q: Name two causes of pathological left ventricular hypertrophy.

children.note: Beyond a limit, hypertrophied myocardium degenerates and fails, leading to heart failure.

manas.q: What happens when cardiac hypertrophy exceeds its limit?

children.note: More cells.
Increase in cell number from proliferation; only possible in tissues whose cells can divide.

manas.q: What does hyperplasia require of a tissue?

children.note: Growth factors drive proliferation of mature cells and new cells from tissue stem cells.

manas.q: What drives cell proliferation in hyperplasia?

children.note: Breast glandular tissue at puberty and in pregnancy; endometrium in the proliferative phase.

manas.q: Give an example of physiological hormonal hyperplasia.

children.note: Liver regrows after partial resection or living-donor liver donation.

manas.q: What is compensatory hyperplasia? Give an example.

children.note: Excess or unopposed oestrogen causes abnormal endometrial hyperplasia; it raises endometrial cancer risk.

manas.q: What causes pathological endometrial hyperplasia and what is the risk?

children.note: Androgen-driven (via dihydrotestosterone) growth of the prostate in older men; not itself a precursor of prostate cancer.

manas.q: Which hormone drives benign prostatic hyperplasia?

children.note: Papillomaviruses cause epithelial hyperplasia seen as skin warts.

manas.q: Which virus causes warts through epithelial hyperplasia?

children.note: Hyperplasia stops when the stimulus is removed, unlike cancer, but it is fertile ground for later malignancy.

manas.q: How does hyperplasia differ from neoplasia?

children.note: Shrinkage of cells, and of the organ, from loss of cell substance.
Reduced cell size from loss of substance; the organ shrinks when enough cells are affected.

manas.q: Define atrophy.

children.note: Less protein synthesis plus more breakdown, mainly by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway.

manas.q: Which pathway breaks down proteins in atrophy?

children.note: Autophagic vacuoles digest cell parts; undigested residue stays as brown lipofuscin pigment ('brown atrophy').

manas.q: What pigment accumulates in atrophic cells?

children.note: Embryonic structures (e.g. thyroglossal duct) and the uterus shrinking after childbirth.

manas.q: Give a physiological example of atrophy.

children.note: Immobilised limb or nerve damage causes skeletal muscle atrophy.

manas.q: How does denervation affect skeletal muscle?

children.note: Slowly reduced blood supply (e.g. ageing brain) or prolonged pressure from a mass causes atrophy.

manas.q: Name two vascular or mechanical causes of atrophy.

children.note: Severe malnutrition (marasmus) wastes muscle; loss of oestrogen after menopause atrophies endometrium and breast.

manas.q: Why does the endometrium atrophy after menopause?

children.note: One adult cell type replaced by another.
Reprogramming of stem or reserve cells, not mature cells changing type, driven by cytokines, growth factors and matrix signals.

manas.q: Which cells are reprogrammed in metaplasia?

children.note: In smokers, ciliated columnar epithelium becomes squamous; tougher but loses mucus and ciliary clearance.

manas.q: What protective function is lost in bronchial squamous metaplasia?

children.note: Squamous metaplasia of endocervical columnar epithelium is normal here, and is where most cervical cancers arise.

manas.q: Where on the cervix does squamous metaplasia occur?

children.note: Lack of vitamin A causes squamous metaplasia of respiratory and conjunctival epithelium.

manas.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes squamous metaplasia?

children.note: Bone forming in soft tissue after injury, e.g. myositis ossificans in muscle.

manas.q: What is myositis ossificans an example of?

children.note: Persistent stimulus can push metaplasia to dysplasia and carcinoma.

manas.q: What can persistent metaplasia lead to?

children.note: Disordered growth, pre-malignant.
Variation in cell and nuclear size, dark large nuclei, more mitoses and loss of normal layering (polarity).

manas.q: List the cell features of dysplasia.

children.note: Graded low or high depending on how much of the epithelium is involved and how atypical it is.

manas.q: How is dysplasia graded?

children.note: Full-thickness dysplasia with an intact basement membrane; not yet invasive.

manas.q: What is carcinoma in situ?

children.note: Low-grade dysplasia may regress if the cause is removed; high-grade lesions carry much higher cancer risk.

manas.q: Can dysplasia regress?

children.note: How adaptations are found.
Tissue biopsy with routine staining confirms hyperplasia, metaplasia or dysplasia.

manas.q: What test confirms metaplasia or dysplasia?

children.note: ECG voltage criteria suggest left ventricular hypertrophy; echocardiography measures wall thickness directly.

manas.q: Which investigations detect left ventricular hypertrophy?

children.note: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsies diagnoses Barrett oesophagus and detects dysplasia.

manas.q: How is Barrett oesophagus diagnosed?

children.note: HPV testing (WHO's preferred primary test), cytology or VIA screen for cervical precancer (CIN) before invasive cancer.

manas.q: Which tests screen for cervical precancer (CIN)?

children.note: When adaptation goes wrong.
Pathological LVH can progress to heart failure and predisposes to arrhythmia.

manas.q: What complications follow pathological LVH?

children.note: Metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma, e.g. Barrett to adenocarcinoma, bronchial squamous metaplasia to squamous carcinoma.

manas.q: Which cancer arises from Barrett oesophagus?

children.note: Prostatic enlargement compresses the urethra, causing urinary outflow obstruction.

manas.q: What is the main complication of BPH?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-18.
Pathological LVH can regress with existing therapies, linked to better outcomes, but under half of patients respond well; exercise and pregnancy hypertrophy fully reverse.

manas.q: Is pathological LVH reversible, per a 2023 review?

children.note: In cardiac hypertrophy, rewired metabolism makes metabolites that directly regulate signalling, transcription and epigenetics, not just energy.

manas.q: Beyond energy, what do metabolites do in cardiac hypertrophy?

children.note: Barrett is linked to older age, male sex, smoking and reflux; about 0.2–0.5% a year develop adenocarcinoma; endoscopic therapy treats most dysplasia.

manas.q: Name risk factors for Barrett oesophagus from a 2022 review.

children.note: Muscle mass depends mainly on synthesis vs breakdown balance; older people show anabolic resistance, so disuse hits them harder.

manas.q: Why are older people more affected by disuse atrophy?

children.note: Quick wins.
Shows both hypertrophy and hyperplasia of smooth muscle, driven by oestrogen.

manas.q: Which two adaptations occur in the pregnant uterus?

children.note: Barrett = squamous to columnar (→ adenocarcinoma); smoker's bronchus = columnar to squamous (→ squamous carcinoma).

manas.q: Contrast the metaplasia in Barrett oesophagus and in a smoker's bronchus.

children.note: Atrophy is shrinkage of a once normal organ; hypoplasia is failure to develop fully.

manas.q: How does atrophy differ from hypoplasia?

children.note: Even carcinoma in situ has an intact basement membrane; invasion through it defines carcinoma.

manas.q: What feature separates carcinoma in situ from invasive carcinoma?

nodeData.note: From the stem cell to every blood cell: the lineages, the growth factors, the marrow tests and what goes wrong. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What haematopoiesis is and why it matters.
The continuous production of all blood cells (red cells, white cells, platelets) from haematopoietic stem cells.

manas.q: What is haematopoiesis?

children.note: Production is huge and constant because most blood cells live only days to weeks and must be replaced.

manas.q: Why must haematopoiesis run continuously?

children.note: At birth almost all marrow is red (active); with age long-bone marrow turns to fatty yellow marrow.

manas.q: How does the distribution of red marrow change with age?

children.note: Yellow marrow can turn back into active red marrow when demand rises, e.g. chronic haemolysis.

manas.q: Can yellow marrow become active again?

children.note: The family tree of blood cells.
Rare marrow cell that can both self-renew and give rise to every blood lineage (multipotent).

manas.q: What two properties define a haematopoietic stem cell?

children.note: Stem cells give a common myeloid progenitor and a common lymphoid progenitor.

manas.q: Which two progenitors arise from the haematopoietic stem cell?

children.note: Myeloid progenitor gives red cells, platelets (via megakaryocytes), granulocytes, monocytes and mast cells.

manas.q: Which cells come from the common myeloid progenitor?

children.note: Lymphoid progenitor gives B cells, T cells and NK cells.

manas.q: Which cells come from the common lymphoid progenitor?

children.note: T-cell precursors leave the marrow and mature in the thymus; B cells mature in the marrow.

manas.q: Where do T cells and B cells mature?

children.note: Stromal cells, osteoblasts, blood vessels and signals such as CXCL12 hold and regulate stem cells.

manas.q: What is the haematopoietic stem cell niche?

children.note: Making red cells.
Proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic normoblast → reticulocyte → mature red cell.

manas.q: List the stages of erythropoiesis in order.

children.note: Cells shrink, fill with haemoglobin and the nucleus condenses then is extruded.

manas.q: What happens to the nucleus during red cell maturation?

children.note: Low tissue oxygen → kidney makes more EPO → marrow raises red cell output → oxygen restored.

manas.q: Describe the erythropoietin feedback loop.

children.note: Needs iron for haem, and vitamin B12 and folate for DNA synthesis in dividing precursors.

manas.q: Which nutrients does erythropoiesis need, and why?

children.note: Making neutrophils and other phagocytes.
Myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band (stab) → segmented neutrophil.

manas.q: List the stages of neutrophil development.

children.note: Marrow holds mature neutrophils ready for release; infection releases them, raising band forms (left shift).

manas.q: What is a 'left shift' on a blood film?

children.note: Monocytes leave the blood and become tissue macrophages.

manas.q: What do monocytes become in tissues?

children.note: Making platelets.
Megakaryocytes copy DNA without dividing, becoming large polyploid cells with lobed nuclei.

manas.q: What is endomitosis in megakaryocytes?

children.note: Platelets are cytoplasmic fragments shed from megakaryocyte extensions into marrow sinusoids.

manas.q: How are platelets released from megakaryocytes?

children.note: Signals that steer production.
Drives neutrophil production and release from the marrow.

manas.q: Which growth factor drives neutrophil production?

children.note: Stimulates granulocyte and monocyte progenitors.

manas.q: Which cells does GM-CSF stimulate?

children.note: Act early on multipotent progenitors; stem cell factor binds c-KIT (CD117).

manas.q: Which receptor does stem cell factor bind?

children.note: Key for early lymphoid (B and T) development.

manas.q: Which cytokine is key for early lymphocyte development?

children.note: Haematopoiesis at the bedside.
Recombinant EPO (or similar agents) treats the anaemia of chronic kidney disease once iron is replete.

manas.q: Why is erythropoietin given in chronic kidney disease?

children.note: Shortens neutropenia after chemotherapy and mobilises stem cells into blood for collection.

manas.q: Give two clinical uses of G-CSF.

children.note: Autologous uses the patient's own cells; allogeneic uses a donor's and risks graft-versus-host disease.

manas.q: What is the difference between autologous and allogeneic stem cell transplant?

children.note: How we judge marrow output.
Hb, red cell indices, white count with differential and platelets show which lineage is affected.

manas.q: What does an FBC tell you about the marrow?

children.note: High after bleeding or haemolysis (marrow responding); low when production fails.

manas.q: How does the reticulocyte count separate production failure from blood loss or haemolysis?

children.note: Shows cell shape, polychromasia (young red cells), blasts, nucleated red cells and left shift.

manas.q: What does polychromasia on a film indicate?

children.note: Nucleated red cells plus immature myeloid cells: suggests marrow infiltration or fibrosis.

manas.q: What does a leukoerythroblastic blood film suggest?

children.note: Usually from the posterior iliac crest; smears show cell morphology and lineage proportions.

manas.q: What is the usual site for bone marrow aspiration in adults?

children.note: Core of bone showing marrow architecture, cellularity, fibrosis and infiltration.

manas.q: What does a trephine biopsy show that an aspirate cannot?

children.note: Aspirate fails to draw marrow, typical of myelofibrosis or packed infiltration; trephine needed.

manas.q: What causes a 'dry tap' on marrow aspiration?

children.note: When production fails or runs wild.
Stem cell failure: pancytopenia with a hypocellular, fatty marrow.

manas.q: What marrow finding defines aplastic anaemia?

children.note: B12 or folate lack impairs DNA synthesis: large red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils.

manas.q: Which blood film finding is typical of megaloblastic anaemia?

children.note: Precursors die in the marrow, e.g. thalassaemia; marrow expands and can widen skull and facial bones.

manas.q: What is ineffective erythropoiesis? Give an example.

children.note: Leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma or metastatic cancer crowd out normal cells, causing cytopenias.

manas.q: How does marrow infiltration cause cytopenias?

children.note: Clonal blasts build up in the marrow and fail to mature, causing marrow failure.

manas.q: Why does acute leukaemia cause anaemia, infections and bleeding?

children.note: Clonal overproduction of mature cells, e.g. polycythaemia vera, often with a JAK2 V617F mutation.

manas.q: Which mutation is common in polycythaemia vera?

children.note: Marrow scarring, teardrop red cells, dry tap and big spleen from extramedullary blood formation.

manas.q: Name three features of myelofibrosis.

children.note: Quick wins.
Low all three lines points to marrow failure, infiltration or hypersplenism.

manas.q: Give three broad causes of pancytopenia.

children.note: Normal in newborns; in adult blood they signal marrow stress or infiltration.

manas.q: When are nucleated red cells in blood abnormal?

children.note: Means the marrow is not responding: check iron, B12, folate, kidneys and the marrow itself.

manas.q: What should you check if anaemia comes with a low reticulocyte count?

children.note: Points that are standard and certain.
WHO cut-offs: Hb below 13 g/dL in men, 12 in non-pregnant women, 11 in pregnancy; WHO's 2024 update uses 10.5 in the second trimester.

manas.q: What are the WHO haemoglobin cut-offs for anaemia in men, women and pregnancy?

children.note: WHO adjusts Hb thresholds upward at altitude; relevant in highland Kenya, including Nairobi.

manas.q: Why are haemoglobin cut-offs adjusted at altitude?

children.note: WHO recommends daily iron and folic acid supplements in pregnancy to prevent anaemia.

manas.q: What supplement does WHO recommend in pregnancy to prevent anaemia?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-18.
With age, mutated stem cell clones make an outsized share of blood; this predicts blood cancers and is linked to higher overall death. Mutant cells can release more inflammatory cytokines.

manas.q: What does clonal haematopoiesis predict, per a 2023 review?

children.note: Stem cells expand in fetal life, stay quiet (quiescent) in adults and decline with ageing, shaped by cell-cycle, inflammatory, epigenetic and metabolic control.

manas.q: How does stem cell behaviour change from fetal life to old age?

children.note: Meta-analysis of 55 trials (406 patients) for inherited disorders: lentiviral vectors engrafted better than gammaretroviral ones, and all 21 genotoxic events were in gammaretroviral trials.

manas.q: Which vector type engrafted better and more safely in stem cell gene therapy trials?

maps.title: HHP 202 · In depth: Overview of the immune system

nodeData.note: Organs, cells and molecules of immunity, self versus non-self, basic tests and main disorders. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What the immune system is and how it is organised.
A network of organs, cells and molecules that defends against infection and abnormal cells while sparing self.

manas.q: What is the immune system?

children.note: Barriers (skin, mucosa), then innate responses, then adaptive responses.

manas.q: What are the three lines of defence?

children.note: Where immune cells are made, trained and meet antigen.
Bone marrow and thymus: lymphocytes are produced and mature there.

manas.q: Name the primary lymphoid organs.

children.note: Lymph nodes, spleen and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT): naive lymphocytes meet antigen.

manas.q: Name the secondary lymphoid organs.

children.note: T cells mature in the cortex and medulla; the thymus is largest in childhood and shrinks after puberty.

manas.q: How does the thymus change with age?

children.note: Cortex follicles hold B cells (germinal centres); paracortex holds T cells; medulla holds plasma cells.

manas.q: Where are B cells and T cells found in a lymph node?

children.note: White pulp holds lymphocytes; red pulp filters blood and removes old red cells and encapsulated bacteria.

manas.q: What are the functions of red and white pulp of the spleen?

children.note: Lymphoid tissue in gut, airways and tonsils, e.g. Peyer's patches in the ileum.

manas.q: Give an example of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

children.note: Who does what (all arise from marrow stem cells).
Most numerous white cell; first to arrive; phagocytose and kill bacteria and fungi.

manas.q: Which white cell is first to arrive at acute bacterial infection?

children.note: Tissue phagocytes from monocytes; eat microbes, present antigen and release cytokines.

manas.q: Name three roles of macrophages.

children.note: Most powerful antigen-presenting cells; carry antigen to lymph nodes to activate naive T cells.

manas.q: Which cells best activate naive T cells?

children.note: Eosinophils fight helminths; mast cells and basophils release histamine in allergy.

manas.q: Which cells release histamine in allergic reactions?

children.note: Make antibody; activated B cells become plasma cells and memory B cells.

manas.q: What do activated B cells become?

children.note: CD4 helper cells coordinate responses; CD8 cytotoxic cells kill infected or abnormal cells.

manas.q: What are the roles of CD4 and CD8 T cells?

children.note: Innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and tumour cells lacking normal MHC class I.

manas.q: Which cells do NK cells kill?

children.note: How self is told from non-self.
Antigen: a molecule the immune system recognises; epitope: the exact part bound by antibody or receptor.

manas.q: What is the difference between an antigen and an epitope?

children.note: On all nucleated cells; shows internal (e.g. viral) peptides to CD8 T cells.

manas.q: Which cells express MHC class I and which T cells read it?

children.note: On antigen-presenting cells; shows peptides from engulfed antigen to CD4 T cells.

manas.q: Which cells express MHC class II and which T cells read it?

children.note: Human MHC is called HLA; it is highly variable and matters in transplant matching.

manas.q: Why is HLA matching important in transplantation?

children.note: Gene segment rearrangement (V(D)J) gives each lymphocyte a unique receptor.

manas.q: How do lymphocytes generate receptor diversity?

children.note: Structure and basic actions.
Two heavy and two light chains; Fab arms bind antigen, Fc stem binds cells and complement.

manas.q: Describe the basic structure of an antibody.

children.note: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD and IgE, set by the heavy chain constant region.

manas.q: Name the five antibody classes.

children.note: Helped by CD4 T cells, B cells switch from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE without changing specificity.

manas.q: What is antibody class switching?

children.note: Chemical messengers between cells.
Small proteins that signal between cells to start, steer and stop immune responses.

manas.q: What are cytokines?

children.note: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF cause fever; IL-6 drives the liver to make CRP.

manas.q: Which cytokine drives hepatic CRP production?

children.note: T-cell growth factor that expands activated T cells.

manas.q: What is the main action of IL-2?

children.note: Not attacking self.
Strongly self-reactive lymphocytes are removed, mainly by deletion, while developing in the thymus (T cells) and bone marrow (B cells).

manas.q: What is central tolerance?

children.note: Regulatory T cells and lack of co-stimulation keep escaped self-reactive cells in check.

manas.q: Name two mechanisms of peripheral tolerance.

children.note: CD4 cells expressing FOXP3 that suppress immune responses.

manas.q: Which transcription factor marks regulatory T cells?

children.note: First tests of immune function.
Counts of neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils and monocytes point to the type of problem.

manas.q: What does a white cell differential tell you?

children.note: Non-specific markers of inflammation; CRP rises and falls faster than ESR.

manas.q: Which inflammatory marker changes faster, CRP or ESR?

children.note: Serum IgG, IgA and IgM screen for antibody deficiency.

manas.q: Which test screens for antibody deficiency?

children.note: Measured by flow cytometry; tracks immune damage in HIV.

manas.q: How is the CD4 count measured and why is it used in HIV?

children.note: Low levels suggest consumption, e.g. in active lupus.

manas.q: What do low C3 and C4 suggest?

children.note: Every patient with recurrent or unusual infections should be offered an HIV test.

manas.q: Which test should be offered to anyone with recurrent unusual infections?

children.note: When the system fails or overreacts.
Too little response: primary (inherited) or secondary (HIV, malnutrition, drugs, cancer).

manas.q: Give three causes of secondary immunodeficiency.

children.note: IgE and mast cells, immediate: anaphylaxis, asthma, hay fever.

manas.q: What mediates type I hypersensitivity?

children.note: Antibody against cell or tissue antigens: haemolytic transfusion reaction, autoimmune haemolysis.

manas.q: Give an example of type II hypersensitivity.

children.note: Immune complexes deposit in vessels and tissues: SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

manas.q: What causes damage in type III hypersensitivity?

children.note: Delayed, T-cell mediated: tuberculin reaction, contact dermatitis.

manas.q: Which cells mediate type IV hypersensitivity?

children.note: Loss of tolerance, e.g. type 1 diabetes, Graves' disease, rheumatoid arthritis.

manas.q: What is autoimmunity? Give an example.

children.note: Recipient's immune system attacks donor tissue, mainly against mismatched HLA.

manas.q: What is the main target in transplant rejection?

children.note: Quick wins.
CD4 × MHC II = 8; CD8 × MHC I = 8.

manas.q: Which MHC class does CD8 recognise?

children.note: No spleen means risk from encapsulated bacteria: pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae b.

manas.q: Which organisms threaten people without a spleen?

children.note: Hypersensitivity types I–IV: Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, Delayed.

manas.q: What does the ACID mnemonic stand for?

children.note: Standard and certain points.
Kenya's national immunisation programme (NVIP, formerly KEPI) gives BCG at birth, in line with WHO advice for high-TB countries.

manas.q: When is BCG given in Kenya's immunisation programme?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-18.
Innate immunity senses microbes via receptors such as Toll-like receptors; its links with adaptive immunity are more complex than simple activation, with cGAS-STING key in infection and cancer.

manas.q: Which innate pathway does a 2024 review highlight in infection and cancer?

children.note: Innate cells can respond more strongly after a past stimulus through epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming; this helps vaccines but may feed heart and inflammatory disease.

manas.q: What is trained immunity, per a 2023 review?

children.note: BCG also gives non-specific protection through monocytes, macrophages and NK cells, with reported benefit in bladder cancer and respiratory viruses; mechanisms not fully clear.

manas.q: Which cells mediate BCG's non-specific protection, per a 2023 review?

maps.title: HHP 203 · In depth: Specimen collection and pre-analytical errors

nodeData.topic: Specimen collection and pre-analytical errors in depth
nodeData.note: From test request to analyser: the right sample from the right patient, in the right tube, in good condition. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What the pre-analytical phase is and why it matters.
Pre-analytical phase: every step before the sample is analysed — test request, patient preparation, identification, collection, labelling, transport, receipt and processing.

manas.q: What steps make up the pre-analytical phase?

children.note: Total testing process: pre-analytical (before testing), analytical (the measurement) and post-analytical (reporting and interpreting the result).

manas.q: What are the three phases of the total testing process?

children.note: The idea that testing starts in the clinician's mind (choosing the test) and ends there (acting on the result); errors can enter at any point of the loop.

manas.q: What does the 'brain-to-brain loop' describe in laboratory medicine?

children.note: A sampling error gives a result that looks real but is not, leading to wrong diagnosis or treatment, repeat sampling and delay.

manas.q: Why are pre-analytical errors dangerous to patients?

children.note: The patient's state when sampled changes the result.
Some tests need fasting, e.g. fasting glucose and triglycerides; a recent meal raises these and can make serum turbid (lipaemic).

manas.q: Name two tests for which the patient should fast.

children.note: Some analytes follow a daily rhythm; cortisol is highest in the early morning, so the sampling time must be recorded and standardised.

manas.q: Why does the sampling time matter for cortisol?

children.note: For therapeutic drug monitoring the timing relative to the dose matters; trough levels are taken just before the next dose.

manas.q: When is a trough drug level taken?

children.note: Standing up shifts fluid out of vessels, so proteins and protein-bound analytes (e.g. calcium) read higher than when lying down.

manas.q: How does posture affect protein and calcium results?

children.note: Strenuous exercise releases muscle enzymes; creatine kinase can be raised after heavy exertion.

manas.q: Which enzyme may be falsely raised after strenuous exercise?

children.note: Wrong patient errors are the most dangerous.
Confirm at least two identifiers (e.g. full name and date of birth or hospital number), asking the patient where possible; never rely on bed number.

manas.q: How should a patient be identified before sampling?

children.note: Label tubes in front of the patient straight after filling; never pre-label empty tubes or label later at the desk.

manas.q: When and where should sample tubes be labelled?

children.note: Blood from one patient labelled as another; in a crossmatch sample it can lead to an ABO-incompatible transfusion.

manas.q: Why is 'wrong blood in tube' especially dangerous for crossmatch samples?

children.note: Details on tube and form must match; labs reject unlabelled or mismatched samples rather than guess.

manas.q: What does the lab do with an unlabelled or mismatched sample?

children.note: Small habits that protect sample quality.
Repeated fist pumping during venepuncture releases potassium from muscle and can falsely raise potassium.

manas.q: How can fist clenching affect a potassium result?

children.note: Avoid an arm with a drip, an arteriovenous fistula, a haematoma or lymphoedema; take from the other arm or below the drip.

manas.q: Which arms or sites should be avoided for venepuncture?

children.note: Very fine needles and forcing blood through a syringe needle into the tube damage red cells and cause haemolysis.

manas.q: How can needle and syringe use cause haemolysis?

children.note: Let the skin antiseptic dry before puncture; wet alcohol stings and can haemolyse the sample, and for cultures drying aids skin decontamination.

manas.q: Why should the skin antiseptic dry before venepuncture?

children.note: Fill additive tubes to the line and invert gently the recommended number of times; do not shake (haemolysis).

manas.q: How should additive tubes be filled and mixed?

children.note: Know the additive, not just the colour: cap colours differ between manufacturers and countries — check your lab's chart.
Binds calcium reversibly; used for coagulation tests (PT/INR, APTT). Blood-to-citrate ratio is 9:1, so the tube must be filled correctly.

manas.q: Which additive is used for coagulation tests and why must the tube be full?

children.note: Blood is allowed to clot, then spun; the fluid is serum. A gel layer, if present, separates serum from cells.

manas.q: What is collected from a plain or clot-activator tube?

children.note: Heparin works through antithrombin to stop clotting; gives plasma for chemistry. Cannot be used to measure a lithium level.

manas.q: Why can a lithium heparin tube not be used for a lithium level?

children.note: Chelates calcium to stop clotting and preserves cell shape; used for full blood count and film, HbA1c and blood bank samples.

manas.q: Name three tests done on EDTA blood.

children.note: Fluoride inhibits enolase, slowing glycolysis; it takes 1–2 hours to act fully, so glucose still falls a little early on. Oxalate is the anticoagulant. Used for glucose and lactate.

manas.q: How does fluoride preserve glucose in a sample?

children.note: Plasma still contains fibrinogen and clotting factors; serum does not. Serum potassium is slightly higher because platelets release it during clotting.

manas.q: What is the difference between serum and plasma?

children.note: The sequence prevents additive carry-over from one tube to the next.
Culture bottles come first to keep them sterile and free of additives.

manas.q: Why are blood culture bottles drawn first?

children.note: EDTA carry-over adds potassium and removes calcium, so it is drawn after serum and heparin tubes.

manas.q: Why is the EDTA tube drawn after serum and heparin tubes?

children.note: With a winged (butterfly) set, a coagulation tube drawn first may underfill because of air in the tubing; a discard tube is drawn first.

manas.q: When is a discard tube needed before a citrate tube?

children.note: The three common sample-quality problems (HIL).
Fine needle, difficult draw, shaking, forcing through a syringe, freezing or long delay of whole blood.

manas.q: List causes of in-vitro haemolysis.

children.note: Haemolysis in the body (e.g. haemolytic anaemia) is real disease; a repeat careful sample that is again haemolysed suggests in-vivo haemolysis.

manas.q: How can you tell in-vivo from in-vitro haemolysis?

children.note: Turbid sample from high triglycerides (e.g. after a meal) scatters light and can cause false results, e.g. pseudohyponatraemia with indirect ion-selective methods.

manas.q: What false electrolyte result can severe lipaemia cause?

children.note: High bilirubin colours the sample and can interfere with some colour-based (photometric) assays.

manas.q: How does icterus interfere with lab tests?

children.note: Analysers measure haemolysis, lipaemia and icterus indices and flag or withhold affected results.

manas.q: What do automated serum indices measure?

children.note: Time, temperature and packaging.
Refrigerating unseparated blood slows the sodium–potassium pump, so potassium leaks out of cells and reads falsely high.

manas.q: Why does refrigerating unseparated blood raise potassium?

children.note: Expel air bubbles and analyse promptly; air in the syringe and delay change the oxygen and carbon dioxide values.

manas.q: How should a blood gas sample be handled?

children.note: Ammonia rises in standing blood; send on ice and analyse quickly.

manas.q: How should an ammonia sample be transported?

children.note: Bilirubin breaks down in light; protect the sample (e.g. neonatal bilirubin) from light.

manas.q: Which common analyte must be protected from light?

children.note: Do not refrigerate; send to the lab promptly for incubation.

manas.q: Should blood culture bottles be refrigerated?

children.note: Leak-proof primary tube, secondary leak-proof container with absorbent, and a rigid outer package (triple packaging) for transport between sites.

manas.q: What is triple packaging for specimen transport?

children.note: Good cultures start at the bedside.
Take cultures before the first antibiotic dose where possible; antibiotics reduce the chance of growing the organism.

manas.q: Why take cultures before antibiotics?

children.note: Yield depends on volume of blood cultured; fill bottles adequately and take more than one set from separate venepunctures.

manas.q: What most improves blood culture yield?

children.note: Pus, fluid or tissue gives better yield than a swab of the surface.

manas.q: Which is better for culture: a swab or pus/tissue?

children.note: Clean-catch midstream urine; send promptly or refrigerate, as bacteria multiply in urine left at room temperature.

manas.q: Why must urine for culture be sent promptly or refrigerated?

children.note: When a result does not fit the patient, think sample first.
High potassium without ECG changes or a cause: think haemolysis, delay, cold storage, EDTA, fist clenching or very high platelets or white cells.

manas.q: List causes of a falsely high potassium.

children.note: Unseparated blood without fluoride, especially with very high white cell counts, consumes glucose before analysis.

manas.q: What can make a glucose result falsely low?

children.note: Clots in an EDTA tube trap platelets and give a falsely low platelet count; poor mixing is a common cause.

manas.q: What does a clotted EDTA sample do to the platelet count?

children.note: Comparing a result with the patient's previous one; a large unexplained change raises suspicion of a sample or identity error.

manas.q: What is a delta check?

children.note: Common reasons: unlabelled or mismatched, wrong tube, clotted, underfilled citrate, haemolysed (for potassium), leaking.

manas.q: Give common reasons for a lab to reject a sample.

children.note: Standards that shape specimen collection.
International standard for quality and competence of medical laboratories; covers the pre-examination process as well as testing and reporting.

manas.q: What does ISO 15189 cover?

children.note: The US Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) venepuncture standard sets the widely used order of draw.

manas.q: Which body's standard sets the widely used order of draw?

children.note: The EFLM Working Group on the Preanalytical Phase (founded 2011) produced a European consensus guideline on venous blood collection.

manas.q: Which EFLM group produced the European venous blood collection guideline?

children.note: WHO guidelines on drawing blood: best practices in phlebotomy (2010) cover safe venepuncture for patients and health workers.

manas.q: Which WHO guideline covers best practice in phlebotomy?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-18.

A 2024 review lists error sources — wrong test requests, poor patient preparation, collection, handling and transport lapses — and controls: harmonisation, training, automated quality checks, lab–clinician teamwork.

manas.q: Name two control measures for pre-analytical errors from a 2024 review.

children.note: A 2023 review notes the pre-analytical phase is now defined to include test selection, to tackle misuse of lab testing, possibly with AI support.

manas.q: Which step has recently been added to the definition of the pre-analytical phase?

children.note: Pre-analytical errors affected care, costs, length of stay and efficiency; standard definitions and education strategies were lacking, and real-world evidence for AI tools was missing.

manas.q: What gaps did a 2025 scoping review find in pre-analytical quality work?

children.note: Quick wins for OSCEs and MCQs.
Think EDTA contamination before treating; repeat the sample.

manas.q: High potassium with very low calcium in a well patient suggests what?

children.note: Too much citrate for the blood volume falsely prolongs PT and APTT.

manas.q: What does an underfilled citrate tube do to clotting times?

children.note: Never use a lithium heparin tube for a lithium level.

manas.q: Which tube must not be used for a lithium level?

children.note: Two identifiers, label at the bedside, never pre-label.

manas.q: What are the two golden rules of sample labelling?

maps.title: HMM 200 · In depth: Bacterial structure and staining

nodeData.topic: Bacterial structure and staining in depth
nodeData.note: How a bacterium is built, why each part matters for disease and antibiotics, and how stains reveal it. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The prokaryotic cell plan.
No nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; DNA lies free in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid.

manas.q: What two features define a prokaryotic cell?

children.note: Cocci (spheres), bacilli (rods), coccobacilli, curved rods (e.g. Vibrio) and spirals or spirochaetes (e.g. Treponema).

manas.q: Name the main bacterial shapes.

children.note: Clusters (staphylococci), chains (streptococci), pairs or diplococci (Neisseria, pneumococcus).

manas.q: Which cocci form clusters and which form chains?

children.note: Membrane, wall and, in Gram-negatives, an outer membrane.
Phospholipid bilayer without sterols (Mycoplasma is the exception); bacteria have no mitochondria, so respiration happens here.

manas.q: Where does energy generation occur in bacteria?

children.note: Sugar chains of alternating NAG and NAM cross-linked by short peptides; gives shape and stops the cell bursting from osmotic pressure.

manas.q: What is peptidoglycan made of and what does it do?

children.note: Beta-lactams block penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) that cross-link peptidoglycan; vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala ends.

manas.q: How do beta-lactams and vancomycin damage the cell wall?

children.note: Enzyme in tears and saliva that cuts the NAM–NAG bond in peptidoglycan — part of innate defence.

manas.q: What bond does lysozyme cut?

children.note: Thick peptidoglycan with teichoic and lipoteichoic acids; no outer membrane.

manas.q: Which acids are unique to the Gram-positive wall?

children.note: Anchored in the membrane; can trigger inflammation and septic shock, in a similar way to LPS.

manas.q: Which Gram-positive wall component can trigger septic shock?

children.note: Thin peptidoglycan in the periplasm between the inner membrane and an outer membrane carrying LPS and porins.

manas.q: Describe the layers of the Gram-negative envelope.

children.note: Gap between the two membranes of Gram-negatives; holds enzymes including beta-lactamases.

manas.q: Where are beta-lactamases found in Gram-negative bacteria?

children.note: Three parts: lipid A (endotoxin), core polysaccharide and the O antigen.

manas.q: What are the three parts of LPS?

children.note: Variable outer sugar chain used to serotype bacteria, e.g. E. coli O157.

manas.q: What is the O antigen used for?

children.note: Endotoxin: lipid A, part of the Gram-negative wall, heat-stable. Exotoxins: proteins secreted by Gram-positives or negatives, often heat-labile.

manas.q: How do endotoxins differ from exotoxins?

children.note: Mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acids in the wall; they stain poorly with Gram and resist drying and many chemicals.

manas.q: What makes the mycobacterial wall acid-fast?

children.note: Parts outside the wall that help bacteria stick, move and hide.
Quellung reaction: capsule swells when mixed with type-specific antiserum (classically pneumococcus).

manas.q: What is the Quellung reaction?

children.note: Most capsules are polysaccharide; Bacillus anthracis has a polypeptide (poly-D-glutamate) capsule.

manas.q: Which bacterium has a polypeptide rather than polysaccharide capsule?

children.note: Loose sugar layer lets bacteria form biofilms on lines, catheters and prosthetic valves (e.g. Staphylococcus epidermidis); biofilms resist antibiotics.

manas.q: Why are device infections with biofilms hard to treat?

children.note: Protein (flagellin) whips for motility; the H antigen. May be single (polar) or all around the cell (peritrichous).

manas.q: What are flagella made of and which antigen do they carry?

children.note: Spirochaetes move by axial filaments (endoflagella) lying under the outer sheath, giving corkscrew motion.

manas.q: How do spirochaetes move?

children.note: Hair-like protein rods for attachment, e.g. uropathogenic E. coli to bladder cells and N. gonorrhoeae to mucosa.

manas.q: What is the main role of common pili?

children.note: Specialised pilus that joins two bacteria for conjugation (DNA transfer).

manas.q: What does the sex pilus do?

children.note: Genetic material, storage granules and spores.
Usually a single circular chromosome, no nuclear membrane.

manas.q: How is the bacterial chromosome organised?

children.note: Small circular DNA that copies itself apart from the chromosome; can carry antibiotic resistance or toxin genes.

manas.q: What clinically important genes can plasmids carry?

children.note: Transformation (taking up free DNA), transduction (via bacteriophage), conjugation (via sex pilus).

manas.q: Name the three ways bacteria exchange genes.

children.note: Volutin (polyphosphate) granules typical of Corynebacterium diphtheriae; shown by Albert stain.

manas.q: Which bacterium has metachromatic granules?

children.note: Formed under nutrient stress, one spore per cell — survival, not reproduction. Core contains calcium dipicolinate, adding heat resistance.

manas.q: Is sporulation a form of reproduction?

children.note: Tetanus, botulism, gas gangrene, C. difficile infection and anthrax.

manas.q: Name diseases caused by spore-forming bacteria.

children.note: Alcohol hand rub does not kill spores; wash hands with soap and water after caring for C. difficile patients.

manas.q: Why use soap and water rather than alcohol gel for C. difficile?

children.note: Spores of Geobacillus stearothermophilus are used as biological indicators to confirm autoclave sterilisation.

manas.q: Which spores test whether an autoclave works?

children.note: Beyond the four reagents.
Thin smear on a slide, air-dried, then heat-fixed before staining.

manas.q: How is a smear prepared for Gram staining?

children.note: Over-decolourising makes Gram-positives look negative; under-decolourising makes Gram-negatives look positive.

manas.q: What error does over-decolourising cause?

children.note: Gram-positives from old cultures or after antibiotics may stain variably as walls weaken.

manas.q: Why may Gram-positives look Gram-variable?

children.note: Report the Gram reaction, shape and arrangement, plus pus cells; gives a fast clue before culture.

manas.q: What does a Gram stain report include?

children.note: Clinical pictures from Gram stains.
Gram-negative diplococci inside pus cells suggest gonorrhoea.

manas.q: What do intracellular Gram-negative diplococci in urethral pus suggest?

children.note: Gram-positive diplococci suggest pneumococcus; Gram-negative diplococci suggest meningococcus.

manas.q: Which organism do Gram-positive diplococci in CSF suggest?

children.note: Mycobacteria (waxy wall), Treponema (too thin), Mycoplasma (no wall), Chlamydia (intracellular).

manas.q: Name bacteria that are not seen well on Gram stain.

children.note: Finding mycobacteria.
Hot carbol fuchsin, then acid-alcohol decolouriser, then methylene blue counterstain; AFB stay red.

manas.q: What are the steps of the Ziehl–Neelsen stain?

children.note: Auramine stains AFB, which glow against a dark background; slides can be scanned faster at lower power, and it is more sensitive than ZN.

manas.q: What advantage does auramine fluorescence have over ZN?

children.note: Uses a weaker acid decolouriser to show weakly acid-fast organisms such as Nocardia and Cryptosporidium oocysts.

manas.q: Which organisms are shown with the modified ZN stain?

children.note: Smear needs many bacilli to turn positive and cannot tell TB from other mycobacteria or show drug resistance.

manas.q: What are the limits of sputum smear microscopy?

children.note: Choose the stain for the organism.
Simple stains use one dye (e.g. methylene blue) to show shape; differential stains (Gram, ZN) sort bacteria into groups.

manas.q: What is the difference between a simple and a differential stain?

children.note: Shows the metachromatic granules of C. diphtheriae.

manas.q: What does Albert stain show?

children.note: Malachite green driven in with heat, safranin counterstain: spores green, cells pink.

manas.q: What colours are spores and cells in a malachite green spore stain?

children.note: Stains the background so a capsule shows as a clear halo; classically for Cryptococcus (a yeast) in CSF.

manas.q: What does India ink staining show?

children.note: Shows live, motile Treponema pallidum in fluid from a syphilitic chancre.

manas.q: How can Treponema pallidum be seen in chancre fluid?

children.note: Structure explains disease and treatment.
Vancomycin is too large to cross the outer membrane, so it does not work on Gram-negatives.

manas.q: Why is vancomycin inactive against Gram-negative bacteria?

children.note: Colistin and polymyxin B bind LPS and disrupt bacterial membranes, so they act on Gram-negatives.

manas.q: What do polymyxins bind?

children.note: Without a spleen, encapsulated bacteria are cleared poorly; vaccinate against pneumococcus, Hib and meningococcus.

manas.q: Which infections threaten asplenic patients and how are they prevented?

children.note: TB microscopy in practice.
WHO recommends LED fluorescence microscopy as an alternative to conventional ZN microscopy for TB smears.

manas.q: Which microscopy does WHO recommend as an alternative to ZN?

children.note: WHO recommends rapid molecular tests (e.g. Xpert MTB/RIF) as the first test for TB; smear microscopy still helps monitor treatment.

manas.q: What does WHO recommend as the initial test for TB diagnosis?

children.note: Papers read 2026-11-18.
A 2023 review notes most current antibiotics target Gram-positives because the Gram-negative outer membrane strongly restricts drug entry; it reviews ways to get past it.

manas.q: Why do many antibiotics fail against Gram-negatives, per a 2023 review?

children.note: Outer membrane porins (e.g. OmpC, OmpF) let in nutrients and some antibiotics; changes in porins reduce entry and contribute to resistance.

manas.q: How do porin changes contribute to antibiotic resistance?

children.note: S. aureus carries at least 18 peptidoglycan hydrolases that keep opening its thick wall for growth and division; they aid virulence and are possible new drug and vaccine targets.

manas.q: What role do peptidoglycan hydrolases play in S. aureus?

children.note: Quick wins for MCQs and practicals.
Gram-positive = purple (crystal violet); Gram-negative = pink (safranin).

manas.q: What colour are Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria?

children.note: On ZN, acid-fast bacilli are red on a blue background.

manas.q: What colour are AFB on ZN stain?

children.note: Lipid A is the toxic (endotoxin) part of LPS; only Gram-negatives have LPS.

manas.q: Which part of LPS is the endotoxin?

children.note: Spores survive boiling and alcohol; autoclaving reliably kills them.

manas.q: What reliably kills bacterial spores?
